questions.q: Flip $n = 4$ fair coins ($p = 0.5$). Using $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$, what is $P(X = 2)$?
questions.explain: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ arrangements, each with probability $0.5^4 = 1/16$, so $6/16 = 0.375$. $0.0625$ forgets the $\binom{n}{k}$ factor (counts only one arrangement).

questions.q: In the Binomial PMF, what does the factor $\binom{n}{k}$ count?
options: The number of different ways to arrange $k$ heads among $n$ flips
The probability that all $k$ chosen flips land heads
questions.explain: $p^k$ and $(1-p)^{n-k}$ give the probability of *one* specific sequence; $\binom{n}{k}$ multiplies by how many sequences have exactly $k$ heads.

questions.q: A biased coin has $p = 0.3$. What is the probability of exactly 3 heads in $n = 10$ flips?
questions.explain: $\binom{10}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^7 = 120 \times 0.027 \times 0.0824 \approx 0.267$. $0.027 = 0.3^3$ ignores both the tails factor and the arrangements.

questions.q: What happens to the Binomial histogram as the number of coins $n$ grows (with $p$ not too extreme)?
options: It becomes increasingly bell-shaped — a hint of the Central Limit Theorem
It always stays perfectly symmetric regardless of $p$
questions.explain: A Binomial count is a sum of $n$ Bernoulli trials, so for large $n$ it looks Normal — fastest when $p$ is near $0.5$. For skewed $p$ it is asymmetric at small $n$.
